question_text: A 54-year-old woman comes to the physician because of paresthesias and weakness in her left leg for one year. Her symptoms have become progressively worse during this period and have led to some difficulty walking for the past month. She has had frequent headaches for the past 4 months. She has a history of hypertension and hypothyroidism. Current medications include amlodipine and levothyroxine. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 97/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows decreased muscle strength in the left lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes of the lower extremity are 4+ on the left and 2+ on the right side. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of electrolytes, glucose, creatinine, and calcium are within the reference ranges. An MRI of the brain is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Question

Deep tendon reflexes of the lower extremity are 4+ on the left and 2+ on the right side. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum concentrations of electrolytes, glucose, creatinine, and calcium are within the reference ranges. An MRI of the brain is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Options

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with progressive neurological symptoms, including weakness and paresthesias in the left leg, along with frequent headaches. The neurologic examination reveals decreased muscle strength and hyperreflexia on the left side, suggesting a possible central nervous system lesion. An MRI of the brain likely indicates a mass effect, necessitating a differential diagnosis that includes primary or metastatic tumors, as well as demyelinating diseases. Given the need for a definitive diagnosis to guide treatment, a stereotactic brain biopsy is the most appropriate next step in management. This approach is minimally invasive and provides essential histological information to determine the nature of the lesion, aligning with standard medical consensus on the management of suspected brain lesions.
